items.title: Everybody hates Pat McAfee
items.content:
here’s an election next week, which means that you and I are currently being bombarded, ceaselessly, with unwanted voices. Here’s one such voice that, alas, we cannot vote out of office come Tuesday:

That’s ESPN commentator and one-man pandemic Pat McAfee. If you’re unfamiliar with McAfee’s work, I envy you. No seriously, if I could trade bodies with you right now, I’d do it in a heartbeat. I don’t even care if you’re 85 and dying of gonorrhea, I’d still do it. That’s just how much I can’t stand Pat McAfee.

Article continues below this ad

And I’m hardly alone. The clip you see up above is McAfee’s response to the harassment (NOTE: term used with ultimate generosity) he endured before co-hosting “College GameDay” for the four-letter live from the Salt Lake City campus of the University of Utah this past Saturday. McAfee is a known quantity to college football fans by now. They know that he’s the former Indianapolis Colts punter who abruptly retired from pro football to take a job for the chauvinist liberation front that is Barstool Sports. They know that McAfee parlayed his Barstool gig into a high-profile radio show where he paid Steelers QB and emotional cancer Aaron Rodgers literal millions of dollars to come on the air with him to muse at length about the dangers of getting vaccinated. And they know that ESPN, desperate to appeal to teenage gambling addicts, scooped up McAfee to become the de facto face of their network, now to the tune of $60 million a year.

They also know that McAfee absolutely, unequivocally sucks.

That’s why, prior to McAfee’s arrival in SLC on Saturday, a few Utah students made a short video of Utes fans doing their best McAfee impressions, which the university found harmless enough to post to its Instagram account (since deleted). I cannot stress how gentle of a ribbing McAfee gets in this video. Even Mitt Romney thinks these kids could have gone in harder on him. But McAfee himself found the video incredibly distressing, so much so that he told his studio bros afterward that he feared for his life going into the belly of the beast!

Article continues below this ad

“The university puts that out? Like as I’m about to go out and do an infomercial for the place? And then I’m walking in front of thousands of these people. This is how the university feels about it? It’s an uncomfortable feeling … I thought to myself, has anything, like, really scary happened at a college gathering in the state of Utah recently?”

McAfee there is referring to the late Charlie Kirk, who was fatally shot while on stage at a campus event at Utah Valley University over a year ago. For reference, the UVU campus is located some 40 miles away from Salt Lake. So why would McAfee instantly think of Kirk getting killed right after a handful of mean and nasty college kids taunted him for always taking his shirt off? Well it’s because, like Kirk, McAfee is a self-absorbed asshole.

Article continues below this ad

And even more galling than McAfee’s inability to tolerate low-ABV jokes from a bunch of Utahns is the fact that ESPN took his security risk comments at face value:

“The safety and security of our on-air team, crew and fans is paramount at ‘College GameDay.’ We are committed to ensuring a safe environment, and given the very real threats that members of our team face, we take issues involving their safety seriously. We support Pat and recognize the very real and valid concerns he has around safety and security.”

According to a report in Front Office Sports, the network apparently feared for McAfee’s safety on the road immediately after Kirk had been shot dead, and the FBI even advised McAfee to wear a bulletproof vest afterward. Although one supposes that McAfee would have simply torn that vest off while on the air to brandish a couple of “guns” of his own.

But even if McAfee was justified to feel skittish about appearing in public crowds, it’s pretty telling how ESPN responded to his concerns with such an outlandish show of force. Because what’s so valid about this man’s safety concerns compared with the concerns of the women he works with, or the women he’s endangered? Are they more valid than the VERY real safety concerns of “GameDay” field reporter Holly Rowe, who was the subject of an AI-generated video of University of Texas head coach Steve Sarkisian punching her in the face ... a video that future fifth-round pick Arch Manning openly laughed about at an official UT presser? Or Mary Kate Cornett, that Ole Miss freshman? After McAfee slandered her on the air to an oblivious Adam Schefter, Cornett’s home was swatted, with armed police knocking down her door. Were either Cornett or Rowe afforded the institutional, DEFCON 1 level response that McAfee got from ESPN (and from the University of Utah!)? Of course they didn’t. That’s because they’re women, and because ESPN didn’t pay either of them $60 million a year to be professionally unfunny 20 hours a day. Even in Donald Trump’s America, the injustice on display is blinding.

Article continues below this ad

There will be no consequences for McAfee from all this. “College GameDay” has enjoyed record ratings since he joined the program (I’d argue this is because college football, not Pat McAfee, is more popular than ever), and ESPN already stood by McAfee in the wake of the Cornett scandal. As far as that network is concerned, there’s big money to be had in cheap trolling. It’s why they pay Stephen A. Smith millions of dollars a year too, after all.

And so, you and I must bear witness to yet another unremarkable man in Pat McAfee failing upward while also clumsily making a martyr of himself. This whiny tank top will never be held accountable for his worst offenses, and he’ll always be shielded by the empty suits working above him. The whole thing is an insult to my intelligence and yours. And I already get my intelligence insulted on a daily basis in this country. Do I really need it from ESPN, too? I’m just trying to watch some football without some wildly self-absorbed, MAGA-coded jackass constantly trying to reach through the TV to suck my brains out. And yet ESPN can’t even afford me, or a handful of clever kids in Utah, that basic courtesy. So I hope that every other “GameDay” crowd from here on out makes Pat McAfee even more uncomfortable than he already is. After all, it’s only fair to return the favor. 

Article continues below this ad

Hearst, the parent company of SFGATE, owns 18% of ESPN.

items.title: The 'best Mexican restaurant in the world' is in SF. It only cost me $500.
items.content:
There is exactly one three-starred Michelin-rated Mexican restaurant in the world, and somewhat rudely, it’s not in Mexico. It’s Californios, a $450 prix fixe gastronomic temple tucked away on 11th Street in the SoMa neighborhood of San Francisco. 

You already know this kind of restaurant simply from the price point (which rose $50 since my visit, from $325 to $375 before tax/tip/drinks), and from the fact that it got the notice of the fabled Michelin judges this year, who went so far as to declare it the best Mexican restaurant in the world. Is this the kind of place custom made for its patrons to boast about having dined there? Of course. Does the 12-course tasting menu include fantasy novel ingredients such as “chickweed”? You bet it does. Do certain dishes come with tweezers? Bitch, you KNOW there are gonna be some tweezers coming your way. As long as epicureanism exists, there will always be establishments like this one: ones that are equal parts thrilling, exhausting and ultra-expensive.

But, knowing what you and I know about the post-COVID world, about the darker side of Michelin-starred kitchens, and about America’s ever-worsening income gap, is the kind of restaurant that dollops caviar onto multiple courses still ? That’s where I come in. Because tonight, I’ll be dining at Californios for the very first time …

Article continues below this ad

I’m not lying when I tell you this restaurant is tucked away. As with so many restaurants of its caliber, Californios, open since 2015, hangs no shingle by its entrance. You have to know it’s there to it’s there, and even then, you can still miss it. I know because I just walked right by Californios’ front door without realizing it, then had to double back as I stared at the pin on Google Maps, then double back again when I walked right by it a second time. This is fine dining as speakeasy: No walk-ins allowed, and the only way in is by securing a reservation months in advance. Again, you and I know this kind of place.

Then I saunter through the main entrance and am instantly transported. I’m standing inside a stone courtyard dotted with luxe wicker patio furniture and potted palm trees. Every muscle in my body slackens. A few steps farther, and now I’m inside a flawlessly lit dining room with walls painted a deep, rich blue and adorned with vibrant paintings that I’d probably pay a separate entrance fee just to stare at. I wish I lived here.

Article continues below this ad

The host escorts me to my table, and I feel a touch sad to be dining alone. This is the kind of place you take her after she’s said yes, you know what I mean? Californios offers romantic ambience in endless abundance. Now I miss my wife. I better stuff myself with 900 pounds of quail mole and black cod tacos to help dull the heartache.

Then I get the menu, and it looks exactly like a wedding program. There’s even a tasteful photograph of a flower affixed to the cover. I half expect to open it and see that my meal will begin with a procession to Vivaldi, followed by a reading from Corinthians. There’s also an autographed welcome card on the table addressed to a “Brodie,” which is not my name but the name of the person who booked my reservation. My server apologizes and promises to get me a new envelope with my actual name on it. I tell them it’s OK. On this night, I’d rather be Brodie. Makes me feel stealthy.

That’s enough prelude. Let’s get to the good stuff, shall we? My evening begins with a flight of aguas frescas: strawberry hibiscus soda, canary melon horchata, and guava/kiwi soda. I also order a separate, a la carte mocktail: a coca noza, Mexican Coke with cherry. All of it is delicious. I love fancy sodas. My appetite has now been sufficiently whetted. I could eat a whole bull right now.

Article continues below this ad

I’ll have to settle for a series of arty small plates instead. As with many other high-end omakase restaurants, dinner at Californios is an overextended affair in which you, the diner, must endure an hourslong procession of courses, each of which includes a little guest lecture from your server before you feel allowed to partake. That waiting can prove a bit torturous, but the tease is part of the burlesque. So I can’t help but groan with pleasure when I finally get to take my first bite: an Anasazi bean sope, or beancake, topped with caviar. I’m a sucker for caviar, and pairing it with this cake, which has been stuffed with a gigante bean mousse, is exactly the stroke of genius I’d expect from chef-owner Val Cantu, who’s originally from Texas and mastered the craft of Mexican cooking during a stint working at Mexico City’s Pujol. I hear another diner say, “This tastes like a memory,” which was surely Cantu’s goal. In this mission, he is fabulously successful. This is food that makes you think, and that makes you to think.

But all that thinking tends to make one hungry. Here comes more modestly sized appetizers — a bluefin tuna tostada that’s been topped with serrano coins and finishes hot on the palate. It’s a slow burn that I hope lingers a good long while. Then comes a single Dungeness crab flauta. I’m a sucker for flautas, too. This is Mexican food all right: instantly recognizable and yet new all at the same time. I want more.

Article continues below this ad

I get it. While sucking down the rest of my coca noza, I’m greeted with a disc of lobster ceviche sitting in a pool of “spicy water,” the latter of which is far tastier than its name implies. The server tells me that I’m free to slurp this aguachile, and I happily take him up on the entreaty. Now here’s abalone on the shell, which I take down in seconds. Every bite here only makes me hungry for more. I suspect that, even after all of these bravura small bites, the Californios kitchen is holding back on the big flavors for the later courses. My patience, admittedly, is wearing a touch thin. The quail mole and rib-eye tacos are still many courses away, and I’m wanting to go to there.

When on my table what should appear but a grilled banana flan topped with serrano ham, date jus, translucently thin plantain chips and, natch, more caviar. I have never tasted anything like this, and likely never will again. In the pre-COVID times, experiential dining like this was revered to the point of absurdity. It feels a bit more crass to enjoy it in a broken 2026 America. But man, eat that flan and tell me if it’s a moral abdication or not. I’m sorry that not everyone gets to try this, but I’m not sorry that get to.

After I lay waste to that savory flan, my server tells me, “Now we’re moving on to tacos.” F—k yeah, we are.

Article continues below this ad

Another showstopper follows: a single fish taco. But this is no ordinary fish taco. Cantu and his staff have battered a rectangle of black cod (aka sable, aka butterfish), placed it atop a sourdough tortilla, and then topped the fish with a corn smut crema and multi-pepper salsa. Frying black cod is a very evil and awesome thing to do. This is the best fish taco I’ve ever eaten, in part because of the aforementioned cod,but also thanks to the sourdough tortilla. I hope sourdough tortillas make it off the runway and down into the retail dining sector sooner rather than later.

It has taken literal hours for me to get through these opening acts, and my back is a touch sore. I get back up to enjoy the courtyard, plus a bathroom that features a toilet with a seat that opens and closes automatically. Makes me feel like a heavy hitter.

Article continues below this ad

the kitchen brings out the big guns. First up is the aforementioned quail mole, which is presented so artfully that I want to hang it on the dining room wall: a diamond-shaped piece of quail breast covered in a mole that surely contains 936 separate ingredients and required 47 hours to make. The mole coats the breast entirely, leaving only a clean matte finish that reflects the light fixtures hanging overhead. To one side of that plate is the leg quarter of that same quail smoked, its lower portion wrapped in twine for easy gripping. To the other side, a bowl of fresh tortillas (not sourdough) crusted in sesame seeds. At certain points during this meal, I kept expecting a burrito to arrive, because I am long conditioned for a specific kind of Mexican food, which, to be clear, kicks major ass. At other points, I’ve wondered if I’d be left so hungry by all these small plates that I would have to go purchase said burrito at another restaurant after  dinner was over. The mole makes all of those cravings and worries disappear. I am being both blown away and sated all in one go.

Ah, but we’re not done yet. Because after the mole comes a final taco, this one stuffed with ribbons of sliced rib-eye that are so tender, they never catch on my teeth. Even better, the kitchen has paired this steak taco with a glass of beet juice (as part of the N/A drink pairings I ordered to go with my tasting menu, at a supplemental cost of $95, now $125) that’s so deep in color and texture that it behaves like red wine. As someone who no longer drinks alcohol and has found all dealcoholized red wines to be rotgut, I’m downright grateful for this glass of beet juice to go with my final taco. I don’t even normally like beets, man. Then again, I am not me tonight. I am Brodie. Brodie will f—k up some beet juice.

Now for dessert. Do they crumb your table before serving you dessert here? You needn’t ask. The main dessert is a chocolate alegría — a kind of traditional Mexican candy — topped with strawberries, lightly toasted amaranth and solidified honey bits. Its satellite desserts include a blueberry empanada and a scoop of almond ice cream, which, when eaten in tandem, is the kind of dessert I would like to eat every night until I’m dead. They spoil you with desserts at Californios, right down to the candied mandarin segments that come with my check. It’s late now, far too late, but I, the mysterious Brodie, will be heading back to my hotel room more than satisfied.

Article continues below this ad

If not conflicted. Again, this is an extremely pricey restaurant. An one. So while I had myself a grand ol’ time at Californios, even without a proper date sitting across from me, I’m still left to wonder if this sort of restaurant can exist in the 21st century, and if it even should. Does the world still need restaurants where the starting price is about the same as a fancy hotel room, where every course comes with its own special set of utensils, and where any question you ask about your food will get you a crisp paragraph in reply? Isn’t this all a bit ostentatious? Do we really want a place like this to still have cultural purchase?

After thinking about it, my answer remains an unequivocal yes. Yes, sitting for an hourslong dinner is kind of an ordeal, and the money spent by customers here would be better spent on helping the destitute, and maybe not every restaurant should have a menu that literally includes pages’ worth of end credits. Would I have preferred to eat all of Californios’ dishes from an a la carte menu, over successive (and much more brief) visits? Of course. But then Cantu’s restaurant might not have gotten quite as much notice from Michelin, which still represents the vanguard of the fine dining establishment. It may not have been recognized as three-star runway food.  

Article continues below this ad

And runway food, of the highest Michelin rating, still needs to exist for the same reason that all high art needs to exist. The world, no matter what condition it’s in, will always need people who feverishly labor to give others something they’ve never experienced before; people who act as credible tastemakers in the greater culture for the coming years, if not decades. That’s especially true in the case of Californios, because it has given Mexican food long-overdue representation in the highest stratosphere of culinary gatekeeping. It’s the first three-star Mexican restaurant in the world, but it will not be the last.
